title: What is known about 1RB1LC_0RC0RB_1LD0LA_1LE---_1LF0LA_1LA0LB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_0RC0RB_1LD0LA_1LE---_1LF0LA_1LA0LB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

The tape holds two binary counters: U, counting up, and V, counting down. Each tick adds 1 to U and takes 1 from V; when V runs out the machine reads a few digits off the bottom of U and writes a new, longer V. That rebuild is now worked out as a function of the counter.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced to an integer map. Lean proves the ticks, any phase of ticks, 38 rebuild rules and one theorem for an infinite family of rebuilds (every k). The whole rebuild is now written in closed form: a walk over pairs of digits of N that collects the subtracted δ term by term (checked against the exact rebuild, not proved). With it the run from blank tape goes through 320,500 rebuilds, more than 1012,000,000 steps, without a halt.

Probably never, but this one stays closer to the edge than its siblings. A halt needs a rebuild with δ = N' + 1, which takes a walk over more than a fifth of the counter. The run keeps producing walks over about 9% of it: each long walk comes back 3.5 times longer after the counter has grown 3.5 times (observed, not proved).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The tick rules of the two counters
claims.text: For each of the headers 0110101, 0110111 the run uses, two theorems: with V odd, L 00000 (00001)^j 00 D>0110101 01 R becomes L 00001 (00000)^j 00 D>0110101 11 R in 10 * j + 34 steps; with V having i + 1 trailing zeros, L 00000 (00001)^j 00 D>0110101 (11)^(i+1) 01 R becomes L 00001 (00000)^j 00 D>0110101 (01)^(i+1) 11 R in 8 * i + 10 * j + 42 steps. That is U + 1 and V − 1 for every number j of carries and i + 1 of borrows and every tape L, R beyond (proved along the symbolic run of tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py).

claims.title: 38 rebuild rules
claims.text: For 38 residue classes of the up-counter N modulo 2j (j in [3, 5, 7], headers 0110101, 0110111) the rebuild after V = 0 is proved for every length n of V and every tape L left of the digits it reads: L dj-1..d0 00 D> H (11)^(n+k) 1 0^inf becomes L 00 D> H' w (01)^(n+e) 1 0^inf, that is: the up-counter loses its lowest j digits (N becomes N >> j) and the new down-counter is 2n+k+c − δ with c and δ fixed by the class. For example, header 0110101 and N = 1 (mod 23): new header 0110101, 8 more digits, δ = 737. The classes were found by sampling; each theorem is then proved along the symbolic run of tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py.

claims.title: Any run of ticks
claims.text: For both headers, every up-counter U (of any width w), down-counter V and every k ≤ V with U + k < 2<sup>w</sup>: k ticks take the tick configuration to the one with U + k and V − k, the widths unchanged and no cell beyond the counters read. Proved by induction on k from the tick rules.

claims.title: The rebuild for a whole family, every k
claims.text: For every k ≥ 1, b in {0, 1}, n ≥ 2k + 3 and every tape beyond: when V = 0 has n digits, the header is 0110101 and the lowest 2k + 3 digits of N are, from the bottom, 2k + 1 ones, a 0 and b, the rebuild ends at the clean tick configuration with up-counter N >> (2k + 3), header 0110101 (b = 0) or 0110111 (b = 1), and a down-counter of n + 5k + 8 digits with value 2n+5k+8 − δ + b, δ = 1 + 32k+1 (3 · 22k+3 − 1). One theorem for the whole family, not one per class: four local passes proved along symbolic runs (lean/Family.lean, written by py/gen_family.py), four phases of 22k − 1 or 22k+1 − 1 ticks by the phase lemma, and two carries into the top word. For k = 1 it is the class N = 7 or 23 (mod 25) of lean/Rebuild.lean (δ = 97281).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 195 cells have been visited and 61 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps (direct)
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c runs 100,000,000,000 steps without a halt (224 cells reached on one side, 104 on the other).

claims.title: The macro map and its simulator
claims.text: At each moment V reaches 0 the tape is the clean configuration 0^inf F U 00 D> H (11)^n 1 0^inf (F the counter's top word), so the state is (H, n, N) with N the up-counter read as one number. py/rebuild.py writes that tape, runs the rebuild (tick runs of its sub-phases jumped by the proved tick rules, the rest cell by cell in C) to the next clean tick configuration (H', n', N', V'), and then adds the V' ticks of the phase by arithmetic: next state (H', n', N' + V'), steps by the closed formula of the tick costs. Tested: its first 7 states and step counts, up to about 10161 steps, equal those of py/counters.py (itself tested against tools/c/tmrun.c).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>17730</sup> steps (macro run)
claims.text: The macro run from blank tape goes through 847 rebuilds without a halt; at the end V has 58,893 digits and the step count is about 10<sup>17730</sup>.

claims.title: The rebuilds that halt, N < 2<sup>16</sup>
claims.text: For every N < 216, both headers, and n − len(N) + 1 in {0, 1} (the only values the run produces, len(N) the number of binary digits of N with the sentinel), the rebuild halts in exactly 22 cases, all with N = 2L+1 − 1 (every digit 1): header 0110101 with L even (n = L or L + 1), header 0110111 with L odd and n = L. The halting step counts grow by a factor 4 per two digits (1727, 6769, 26787, ... for header 0110101, n = L + 1). Every other rebuild returns to a clean tick configuration.

claims.title: A halting configuration two rebuilds away
claims.text: For N < 214 (same inputs) the rebuild always gives N' = N >> j for some j, or N' = 2, and N' − δ = −1 (the next counter N' + V' all ones) only for N = 5885 and 5889, n = 12, 13, header 0110101. For N = 5889, n = 13 that all-ones counter has the halting parity: the tape 1 [5889 in 5-cell digits] 00 D>0110101 (11)^13 1, run directly by c/fromtape.c, halts after 545,221,856 steps (a rebuild, 221 − 737 ticks, a halting rebuild), the same count as the macro simulator's. So the machine can halt from configurations of its own family; the question is whether the run from blank tape reaches one.

claims.title: Where every rebuild stops: a walk over pairs of digits
claims.text: The rebuild reads N's digits from the bottom in pairs b2i+1b2i and moves a 4-state automaton (table on the explainer page); header 0110101 starts it in O, 0110111 in Q. If it stops on its k-th pair, j = 2k + 1 digits are read, N' = N >> j, the new header is 0110101 or 0110111 by the last digit read, and V gains c = (5j + 1)/2 digits. Compared with the exact rebuild of py/rebuild.py: for every N < 216, both headers and n − len(N) + 1 in {0, 1}, 151,368 rebuilds follow it and none contradict it; 110,768 are not covered (the walk does not stop below the top digit of N). For 2,000 random 200-digit N, both headers, all 4,000 follow it (longest walk j = 127). In the macro run from blank tape, 940 of the first 941 rebuilds follow it (longest walk j = 5,015); the other one, rebuild 5, is not covered: its walk reaches the top of N (it read 80 of the 82 digits and left N' = 2). The automaton was read off the data; it is not proved.

claims.title: The rebuild in closed form
claims.text: The rebuild written out completely as a function of the macro state: (h, n, N) goes to (b, n + c, 2n+c + (N >> j) − δ), c = (5j + 1)/2, where j, b and δ come from one pass over the pairs of digits of N from the bottom, in mode O (header 0110101) or Q (0110111). Pairs are written upper digit first, and k counts the pairs 11 skipped since the last term. O, pair 01: stop, b is the next digit, last term 1 − b + 25k+5(3·22k+3 − 1). O, 00: term (3·22k+2 − 1) 25k+5, subtract 1 from the rest of the counter, stay in O. O, 10: the same term, go to Q. Q, 00: term A, subtract 1 from the rest, stay in Q. Q, 10: term A + 10, subtract 1 from the rest, go to O. Q, 01: term B, subtract 1 from the rest, go to O. Here A = 27k+9 − 3·25k+6 and B = 27k+10 − 3·25k+6 − 2, and directly after a Q-00 step A = 27k+10 − 25k+7, B = 27k+11 − 25k+7 − 2. δ is the sum of the terms, each shifted left by 5 places per pair read after it. So the states P and R of the 4-state walk are O and Q with a borrow pending on the counter. The terms were fitted to computed rebuilds and then compared with the exact rebuild: all 1,582 classes of low digits with j ≤ 14 (both headers), each with two values of n; 1,500 random 300-digit counters (longest walk j = 75); rebuilds 8 to 300 of the run from blank tape. No difference. The formulas are not proved.

claims.title: The reduction: halting iff δ = N' + 1 once
claims.text: If the halting rebuilds are the all-ones ones for every N (checked below 216), then, since the next counter is N' + V' = 2n' + N' − δ, the machine halts if and only if some rebuild of the run gives δ = N' + 1 with new header 0110101 and n' odd. A rebuild of a proved class has a fixed δ (at most 24 digits for j ≤ 7) and N' = N >> j, so once N has more than 31 digits (from the second rebuild on) only the classes not yet in Lean (j ≥ 9) can do it.

claims.title: What the rebuild map looks like in the run
claims.text: All 847 rebuilds of the macro run have N' = N >> j. j is odd except once (rebuild 5 read 80 of the 82 digits) and then the new V has c = (5j + 1)/2 more digits than the old. The number of digits read has a long tail (84 with j = 3, 108 with j = 5, 83 with j = 7, 77 with j = 9, 61 with j = 11, 54 with j = 13; up to j = 2481), like the stopping time of a random walk on the digits. From rebuild 7 on, N' always has at least 301 more digits than δ (the gap grows with n), so δ = N' + 1 never came close.

claims.title: Probably never halts
claims.text: δ has about 2.5j to 3.5j digits and N' about len(N) − j, so δ = N' + 1 needs a rebuild that reads about a quarter of the counter and then an exact match of the remaining three quarters, digit for digit. Treating those digits as random, that has probability about 2<sup>−0.7 n</sup> at a rebuild with n digits; n is over 45 from the third rebuild on and grows by about 70 per rebuild, so the sum over the whole run is tiny. A heuristic, not a proof: the digits of N are produced by the machine, not drawn at random.

claims.title: 320,500 rebuilds of the map without a halt
claims.text: If the closed map is the rebuild for every counter (checked on the cases listed there, not proved), the run from blank tape goes through 320,500 more rebuilds after the seventh without a walk that reaches the top of the counter. At the end V has 41,132,351 digits, so the machine has run more than 10<sup>12,000,000</sup> steps. A halt needs δ = (N >> j) + 1; after the first 1,000 rebuilds δ was never longer than 0.34 of the length of N >> j, and no rebuild had δ > N >> j. This run is much shorter than those of the two sibling machines (10<sup>8</sup> rebuilds) because the long walks below make the low part of the counter millions of digits long.

claims.title: Long walks come back 3.5 times longer
claims.text: Unlike its two open siblings this machine keeps making walks that read a fixed share of the counter. Observed in that run: a walk of j digits leaves a gap of (7j − 1)/2 zeros below the new top digit; when the δ of a later long walk ends inside such a gap, the borrow turns the rest of the gap into a block of ones; when the block reaches the low end one walk reads all of it and a little more. Meanwhile the counter has grown 3.5 times as well, because every digit read adds 2.5 digits on top. So the long walks form chains: 5,015, 19,303, 69,007, 242,225, 848,077, 2,968,733 digits, each about 3.5 times the one before and each reading 8.7% to 8.9% of the counter at that moment; a second chain runs 7,237, 24,695, 86,021, 302,021. Between the blocks the counter is isolated ones with gaps of 7k + 3 zeros, and a walk crossing them stops at the first or second 1 that sits in the upper place of a pair, so it goes only a few gaps beyond its block (in the cases looked at). A halt would need a walk that reads more than a fifth of the counter (δ has up to 3.5j digits and must be as long as the rest) and then an exact match of the rest. None of this is proved; it explains why the share stays constant but does not bound it.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Lean proves the ticks, any phase of ticks, 38 short rebuild classes and one family of rebuilds for every k. The whole rebuild is now written in closed form (checked against the exact rebuild, not proved in Lean). What is missing is a proof of that map and, above all, an invariant of the counter that keeps every walk away from its top: the long walks keep reading about 9% of the counter, generation after generation, and nothing proved prevents a longer one.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt with the closed rebuild map (checked, not proved); 10<sup>17730</sup> steps in the exact macro simulation.
Rebuild rules proved in Lean for every n.
One Lean theorem for an infinite family of rebuilds.

sections.heading: Two binary counters on one tape
html: Run the machine for a while and the tape sorts itself into two numbers written in binary. On the far left, after a single 1 that acts as a sentinel, is a counter U whose digits are blocks of 5 cells: 00000 is a 0 and 00001 a 1, most significant digit on the left. Then come a short gap 00, the head in state D, and a fixed header such as 0110101. Right of the header is a second counter V whose digits are pairs, least significant first: 01 is a 1 and 11 a 0.
The tick configuration is 1 U 00 D>0110101 V. Every tick adds 1 to U and takes 1 from V. Most of the time nothing else happens.

sections.heading: One tick: U + 1, V − 1
html: The head walks left through the trailing 1-digits of U, turning them into 0-digits (the carries), writes a 1-digit, then walks right to V and turns its trailing 0-pairs into 1-pairs and its lowest 1-pair into a 0-pair (the borrows). Written with j carries and i + 1 borrows:

beforeaftersteps
L 00000 (00001)^j 00 D>0110101 01 RL 00001 (00000)^j 00 D>0110101 11 R10 * j + 34
L 00000 (00001)^j 00 D>0110101 (11)^(i+1) 01 RL 00001 (00000)^j 00 D>0110101 (01)^(i+1) 11 R8 * i + 10 * j + 42

These two shapes are proved in Lean for every j and i (lean/Rules.lean), for every header the run has used (0110101, 0110111). Because the cost of a tick depends only on the numbers of carries and borrows, a long run of ticks has an exact cost: the sum of the trailing zeros of the numbers U+1, ..., U+k and V−k+1, ..., V, which has a closed form. The accelerated simulator uses it to skip billions of ticks at once.

sections.heading: The rebuild as a function of the counter
html: When V reaches 0 the tape is always clean: 0^inf 1 U 00 D>H (11)^n 1 0^inf, nothing else on it. Read the up-counter with its sentinel 1 as one binary number N (U = 5287 with 13 digits is N = 213 + 5287). The state of the whole machine is then just (H, n, N): the header, the length of V and the counter.

The rebuild that follows reads the lowest digits of N one at a time, writing to the right, and stops after j of them, where j depends on what it read. It ends in a clean tick configuration again: the up-counter is N' = N >> j (the digits it did not read), and the new V is 2n+c − δ, nearly all 1-pairs, with c and δ fixed by the digits read. For the short cases this is proved in Lean (38 theorems), for example:

sections.heading: The rebuild's stopping rule: a walk over pairs of digits
html: Which digits a rebuild reads is decided by a small automaton. Cut N into pairs of digits from the bottom, b1b0, b3b2, ..., and walk through this table, starting in O after header 0110101 and in Q after 0110111:

statepair 00011011
OPstopQO
PPPstopQ
QRPPQ
RRRPP

If the walk stops on its k-th pair, the rebuild has read j = 2k + 1 digits: N' = N >> j, the next header is 0110101 or 0110111 according to the last digit read, and V gains (5j + 1)/2 digits. This matches the exact rebuild for every N below 216 and for thousands of random 200-digit counters, but it is read off the data, not proved.

The simplest walk stays in O on 11-pairs and stops on 01: N ends in 2k + 1 ones, a 0 and a digit b. For that whole family Lean proves the rebuild for every k at once: four short passes, four runs of 22k − 1 or 22k+1 − 1 ticks and two carries, ending with δ = 1 + 32k+1 (3 · 22k+3 − 1). For other walks δ also depends on how long the runs of equal pairs are, and the rebuild sometimes runs a smaller rebuild inside itself; the next section gives a formula for every walk (checked, not proved). There is no proof that the machine never halts.

sections.heading: Try the rebuild on any counter
html: The whole rebuild can be written out. The formulas were fitted to computed rebuilds and agree with the exact rebuild on every case tried; they are not proved. Type a counter in binary and choose the header; the page shows the walk, the subtracted δ and the next counter. The counter filled in is the one of the run from blank tape after its seventh rebuild (722 digits, header 0110101); the second button follows the run from there.

The walk has two modes and a borrow. Pairs 11 are skipped. In O a pair 01 stops the walk, 00 gives a term and a borrow, 10 gives a term and changes to Q. In Q every other pair gives a term and a borrow; 00 stays in Q, the mixed pairs go back to O. A borrow means: subtract 1 from the rest of the counter, so the following 00 pairs read as 11 and the first other pair is lowered by one. The states P and R of the table above are O and Q with a borrow pending. δ is the sum of the terms, each shifted 5 places per pair read after it, and the next counter is 2n' + (N >> j) − δ.

In the run the long walks come in chains. A walk of j digits leaves a gap of (7j − 1)/2 zeros at the top of the counter. Later the borrow of another long walk turns most of that gap into a block of ones, and when the block arrives at the bottom a single walk skips through all of it. By then the counter is 3.5 times longer too. Observed chain: 5,015, 19,303, 69,007, 242,225, 848,077, 2,968,733 digits, always about 9% of the counter. A halt needs more than a fifth and then an exact match. Nothing proved keeps the share where it is.

sections.heading: Halting, reduced to the rebuild map
html: The machine halts only on D reading a 1, and ticks never do that. Running every rebuild with N < 216 shows exactly which halt: the ones where every digit of N is 1 (N = 2L+1 − 1), with the right parity of L and header. Since the next counter is 2n' + N' − δ, it is all ones exactly when δ = N' + 1. So halting comes down to one arithmetic coincidence at some rebuild.

It can happen: from 1 [N = 5889] 00 D>0110101 (11)^13 1 the rebuild gives N' = 736, δ = 737, the counter fills up to 221 − 1 and the next rebuild halts, after 545,221,856 steps in all (checked by direct simulation).

In the run from blank tape it looks hopeless: from the seventh rebuild on N' has at least 301 more digits than δ, and the gap grows. A coincidence needs a rebuild that reads about a quarter of the counter and then a digit-for-digit match of the rest, roughly a 2−0.7n chance with n in the thousands. That is why we believe it never halts, but there is no proof: it would need the rebuild for every N, not just the short cases in Lean.

family: Up/down two counters with resets (G12 family 3b)
